s1a.text: On January 1st, 2027, California bans food with Red No. 3. There's no sell-through period.

s1b.text: The dye hides under many names: erythrosine, E127, "Red 3", even scanning typos. It's in hundreds of products, on thousands of shelf spots, and stores get one overnight shift to clear it.

s1c.text: Miss one, and it's a violation. Pull the wrong one, since Red 40 looks almost the same on a label, and you empty shelves for nothing. Our simulated drill is for a large big-box retailer with nearly 300 California stores.

k1b.text: Gemini 4 Argon wrote this working system this morning, in one generation. Here it runs on 20 of those stores, overnight.

k2.text: Inside a store, flashing tags are pulls still to do. Associates walk to each shelf, pull the product, and put a substitute in its place.

k3b.text: Every decision shows its evidence: erythrosine found, a vague "artificial color" held for a person, a Red 40 look-alike left on the shelf.

k4b.text: It found all 467 products with Red No. 3, pulled 0 of the 483 look-alikes, and covered all 6,718 shelf spots, with 0 plan mistakes. 1 extra item was pulled, one our rules say to check by hand.

k6b.text: Argon's first draft missed 25 of the 467, leaving 350 shelf spots with banned product. Three small logged fixes closed the gap.

z1b.text: Simulated drill, simulated operations, every number from the verifier.

s2.text: That's hard for software. A compliance pull isn't one program. It's many parts that must agree: reading labels, the law's dates, every shelf location, who works which shift, which substitute goes where, which truck takes the returns. Written in pieces, those pieces drift apart at the seams.

s3_exp1.text: Gemini 4 Argon can hold the whole system in one continued generation. In our experiment it wrote about 254,000 tokens of code, 314 files, and every one of its 2,838 cross-file links lines up. That's the point of a million-token model: the whole system in one head.

s3b_exp1.text: Here's its longest link: a file written early, used by a test near the end. Its tests pass, live.

s4_exp1.text: But consistent code isn't correct code. Our verifier ran the plan and found 8,441 mistakes. Each row here is one simulated associate. Red means Argon's plan sent the same person to two shelves at once: 7,631 double-bookings across 20 stores.

s5a.text: A managed agent read the verifier's findings, found the 2 root causes, and fixed them. Mistakes went from 8,441 to 0, including in 10 stores it never saw.

s5b.text: And the working core Argon wrote this morning, on 20 stores, overnight: tags flash, associates walk to each shelf, and every store goes green.

s5c.text: With three small logged fixes to its first draft, it found all 467 products with Red No. 3, pulled none of the 483 look-alikes, covered every one of 6,718 shelf spots, and finished every task before midnight.

p1.text: At midnight on January 1st, 2027, every product in California with Red No. 3 becomes illegal to sell. No grace period.

p1b.text: The dye hides under many names. Stores get one night.

p2.text: Reading a label decides what's pulled. What's pulled decides which shelves, which people, which shifts, which substitutes, which trucks. Change one rule and it ripples through all of them. A system like this has to agree with itself, everywhere at once.

p3.text: So we asked Gemini 4 Argon to write the whole system in one continued generation: one author, holding every part in mind at once.

p3a.text: 646,825 tokens. 911 files. Ten hops, nine hand-offs, every one clean.

p3b.text: After a one-line fix, all 6,581 cross-file links line up.

p3c.text: A test written at token 641,687 calls a function Argon wrote 552,000 tokens earlier.

p3e.text: That's what a million-token model is for: the whole system in one head.

p4.text: But consistent code isn't correct code. Our verifier found 21,459 plan mistakes: people double-booked, tasks outside the shift.

p5.text: A managed agent traced it to one root cause and fixed it. Scheduling mistakes went to zero, even in stores it never saw.

p6.text: When a law changes overnight, you don't have months. Argon writes the whole system at once, the verifier proves it, the agent repairs it.
